text:
I get asked a lot about what happens inside a popcorn kernel, and my answer is simple: it is mostly a tiny explosion of trapped steam. A kernel looks like a small hard bead, but the outside is a sealed shell, and inside there is starchy endosperm with a little moisture. When you heat the kernel, that moisture becomes superheated water under pressure. It is not a gentle cooking process; the shell is holding back a rapidly rising pressure until it fails. That failure is the crack you hear. Once the shell gives way, the starchy material expands almost instantly into the white, airy part we eat.
What I find interesting is that the same shell that makes popping possible also prevents the kernel from releasing steam gradually. Without that sealed container, the water would just evaporate and the kernel would dry out. The shell has to withstand a surprising amount of pressure, and the popping sound is the shell splitting rather than the starch deciding to grow. I think that makes a nice contrast with ordinary bread or cereal puffs, where expansion is slower and controlled. Here the expansion is violent and brief, which is why a batch of popcorn can fill a bowl so quickly.
I also like how the result depends on moisture content. A kernel that is too dry will not pop because there is not enough water to build enough pressure. If it is too wet, it may puff up or make a mush instead of popping cleanly. Good popping kernels have the right balance: enough water to create steam pressure, and enough starch to form that soft, expandable mass. I have popped it for years and still find the popping sound oddly calming, but the mechanism inside is not calm at all.
For me, the most satisfying part is that the kernel is doing something surprisingly mechanical. It is not magic. Heat turns water into pressurized steam, the shell bursts, and starch gelatinizes and expands. The white cloud you see is starch turning into a solid foam, almost like a tiny puffed up version of the kernel interior. That is why the popped kernel is puffy and white: the starch structure has set in an expanded state. So if you are wondering what is actually happening inside, it is trapped steam doing most of the work, with the shell deciding when it finally lets go.
